reflection.quote: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.
reflection.reading:
Mondays used to feel like punishment. Hungover, scraping together an excuse for being late, promising myself Friday would be different this time. Monday was proof that the weekend had happened to me instead of being lived by me.

Sobriety changed what Monday is. It's just a day now. You get up, you make coffee, you go do the thing. Nothing dramatic. The alarm isn't an interrogation. You remember your conversations from the weekend. Your body isn't filing a formal complaint. There's a strange, understated power in that — the fact that an ordinary Monday is actually available to you. For years it wasn't. You were somewhere else when it showed up, or you were trying to survive it.

Durant's line about habit gets misquoted into a productivity slogan, but the real weight of it is quieter. You become what you do on the days nobody is watching. Not the big recovery milestones, not the anniversaries — the Tuesday grocery run, the Monday morning shower, the walk you take because you said you would. This is where the person you can live with gets built. Not in a single decision to get sober, but in a thousand small Mondays where you show up on time, pay attention, and don't disappear. One day at a time means today. This one. The Monday one.
reflection.meditation: What's one small, ordinary thing I can do today — on purpose, with my full attention?

affirmations: I am present for this Monday in a way I couldn't be before.
Today I build the life I want in small, unglamorous choices.
I am becoming someone I can actually live with.

gratitude.prayer: Grateful for a Monday I can remember. Grateful for a body that isn't begging me to stop, a mind clear enough to plan the week, and the quiet luxury of an ordinary morning. There was a long stretch where none of this was available to me, and I don't want to forget that.
gratitude.closing: One ordinary day. That's the whole gift.
